body_text: PDF Version REDWOOD CITY, Calif., May 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Jasper Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: JSPR) (Jasper), a clinical stage biotechnology company focused on development of briquilimab, a novel antibody therapy targeting c-Kit (CD117) to address mast cell driven diseases such as chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) and asthma, today reported results for the fiscal quarter ended March 31, 2026 and provided a corporate update. "In recent months, we have continued to advance the briquilimab development program in CSU," said Jeet Mahal, President and Chief Executive Officer of Jasper. “Following our positive clinical data update in January, we have conducted an analysis of the full data package from BEACON, SPOTLIGHT and the open-label extension study to drive the selection of two active dosing regimens to evaluate in our Phase 2b study. In parallel we have also updated and refiled the Phase 2b protocol with the FDA as we work to secure additional funding to enable commencement of the study in the second half of this year as planned.” Highlights for First Quarter 2025 and Recent Weeks Refiled an updated Phase 2b protocol with the FDA for the planned Phase 2b study of briquilimab in CSU. Jeet Mahal appointed as Chief Executive Officer to lead next phase of clinical growth. Reported positive updated data from briquilimab studies in chronic spontaneous urticaria in January 2026: 67% of additional patients (n=6) enrolled in the BEACON study given an initial dose of 240mg briquilimab followed by 180mg every 8 weeks achieved a complete response at 12 weeks with a mean UAS7 reduction of 31 points 75% of CSU participants (n=36) enrolled in the open label extension dosed with 180mg briquilimab every 8 weeks achieved a complete response or well controlled disease at 12 weeks With a median duration of follow up of more than 200 days on 63 participants in the open label extension study, KIT related AEs were low in frequency and predominantly low-grade events that resolved while on study First Quarter Fiscal 2026 Financial Results Cash and cash equivalents as of March 31, 2026, totaled $14.1 million. Research and development expense for the three months ended March 31, 2026, was $5.8 million. General and administrative expense for the three months ended March 31, 2026, was $5.1 million. Jasper reported a net loss of $1.2 million, or basic and diluted net loss per share attributable to common stockholders of $0.04 for the three months ended March 31, 2026. About Jasper Jasper is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing briquilimab as a therapeutic for chronic mast cell diseases. Briquilimab is a targeted aglycosylated monoclonal antibody that blocks stem cell factor from binding to the KIT receptor, thereby inhibiting signaling through the receptor. This inhibition disrupts the critical survival signal, leading to the depletion of the mast cells via apoptosis which removes the underlying source of the inflammatory response in mast cell driven diseases such as chronic urticaria and asthma. Jasper is currently evaluating briquilimab as a treatment in patients with CSU, CIndU and asthma. Briquilimab has a demonstrated efficacy and safety profile in patients and healthy volunteers, with positive clinical outcomes in CSU, CIndU and allergic asthma. For more information, please visit us at www.jaspertx.com . title: Caso de éxito Soprole: Cómo Soprole transformó la debida diligencia de sus proveedores
summary: Cómo Soprole transformó la debida diligencia de sus proveedores con Plutto. Entrevista a Daniela Zuleta, Paloma Lara y Marlene Montoya del área de abastecimiento.
body_text: Caso de éxito En resumen Cuando una empresa como Soprole busca un partner para su due dilligence, lo hace de forma profesional. Sus decisiones deben estar bien fundamentadas, por eso decidieron analizar cinco proveedores distintos. Por qué eligieron Plutto "Tres de ellos los llevamos a piloto y la facilidad (en el uso) que mostraba Plutto sobre las otras alternativas, fue lo que nos llevó a tomar la decisión de trabajar con ellos." Con empresas automatizando sus procesos internos en todo el mundo, Soprole requería mantenerse en la vanguardia. Por eso, la posibilidad de unir procesos era una de las razones principales para buscar un partner como Plutto. Así lo explica Daniela Zuleta. "Queríamos poder evaluar a nuestros proveedores de mejor manera, porque hasta antes de Plutto podíamos evaluarlos en procesos desagregados, pero no de manera integral." El impacto en los procesos Actualmente, Plutto reduce en un 80% el tiempo dedicado a los procesos de debida diligencia que antes se realizaban manualmente. Esto permite agilizar operaciones, asignar talento a tareas de mayor valor y generar un ahorro significativo en la operación. A eso sumémosle que la integración de Plutto a las operaciones diarias es muy fácil: "El proceso de implementación ha sido bastante rápido. A los pocos días ya no era necesario que desde las distintas áreas coordinásemos por correo las aprobaciones para los proveedores." Esta es otra de las características más valiosas de Plutto: todo el proceso lo llevas en un solo lugar. Velocidad para encontrar información Marlene Montoya, líder de negociación estratégica, entiende que la rapidez con que Plutto busca y encuentra información está haciendo una diferencia importante dentro de sus procesos. "Hemos ahorrado mucho tiempo en buscar información sobre las empresas que son nuestros proveedores. Antes, con el proceso manual, esa investigación era muy lenta. Hoy nos basta ingresar el rut para tener la información que requerimos en nuestros procesos para validar a un nuevo proveedor." ¿Por qué es relevante este punto? Porque si tu empresa no tiene Plutto, buena parte de esta información llega desde los mismos proveedores, lo que genera puntos ciegos en la evaluación de los mismos. Lo que viene Para Soprole ahora el desafío que viene es integrar esta tecnología a todos los procesos, generando KPIs que permitan hacer seguimiento, generar métricas, evaluar procesos y seguir mejorándolos. Entonces ¿recomendarías Plutto? "Sí, lo recomiendo por su facilidad en el uso, por la flexibilidad y la comunicación constante con el equipo. Siempre están dispuestos a buscar nuevas formas de hacer las cosas y adaptarse a las empresas con las que trabajan." Mira la entrevista completa ¿Quieres simplificar la evaluación de tus proveedores? Conversa con nuestro equipo y te mostramos cómo Plutto puede integrar y acelerar tu proceso de debida diligencia. Conversa con nuestro equipo →

title: Using Attendee Data to Program Panels That Fill Seats Year After Year
summary: Discover how data-driven convention panel scheduling can pack your event’s rooms every year. Learn practical ways to collect & analyze attendee data – fr...
body_text: Why Data-Driven Convention Panel Scheduling Matters Fan convention panel scheduling can make or break an event’s success. In an era where major cons host hundreds of panels and activities, using attendee data to guide programming is no longer optional – it’s essential. The biggest fan events, from San Diego Comic-Con’s 135,000+ attendees to New York Comic Con’s record 180,000 tickets sold , illustrate the stakes: packed panels lead to engaged, satisfied fans, while empty rooms or overcrowded halls signal missed opportunities. Convention veterans have learned that data-driven event programming isn’t just a buzzword; it’s a competitive edge that keeps fans coming back every year. Attendees vote with their feet at conventions – showing up for content they love and skipping what doesn’t interest them. By analysing which sessions draw big crowds and which fizzle, organisers can continuously refine their schedules. For example, Anime Expo 2024 in Los Angeles featured around 400 panels, screenings, and events over four days. With such breadth of content, a data-driven approach is crucial to allocate popular panels to bigger rooms, schedule them at optimal times, and ensure niche topics find their passionate audiences. Simply put, leveraging attendee data helps fill seats year after year by aligning programming with fan demand. Visualizing Your Convention Pulse — Mapping out peak activity times helps you anchor your schedule with high-impact sessions when attendee energy is highest. Beyond improving fan satisfaction, data-informed panel scheduling makes economic sense. Packed rooms often mean higher on-site spending and happier sponsors, exhibitors, and guests. Conversely, consistently half-empty panels waste resources and can dampen the event atmosphere. As recent convention industry trends highlight , technology is enabling organisers to fine-tune experiences based on real-time insights. Leading fan events worldwide – whether a 2,000-person local anime con or a 100,000+ attendee expo – are embracing data to drive decisions. The result? More must-see panels, fewer scheduling misfires, and a reputation that keeps attendees excited for next year. Collecting Attendee Data: From Registration to Panel Rooms Data-driven panel programming starts with collecting the right attendee data. To truly understand what your fans want, you’ll need reliable metrics on how they engage with your content. This means gathering information at every stage – from pre-event surveys and registration info to on-site attendance counts and post-event feedback. Here’s how veteran organisers capture data to inform their panel scheduling: Data-Driven Event Marketing Track ticket sales, demographics, marketing ROI, and social reach in real time. Exportable reports give you the insights to make smarter decisions. Event Data Analytics Software Try It Free Tracking Panel Attendance and Participation The foundation of data-driven scheduling is knowing how many people attend each panel and who they are. Manual headcounts can work for intimate events, but larger cons benefit from technology to track attendance accurately. Many conventions use badge scanning or RFID tracking at panel room entrances to log attendee counts in real time. For example, some events issue RFID-enabled badges and have attendees tap in at each session – yielding precise headcounts and even insights into individual attendee preferences. Modern convention registration systems (such as a dedicated pop culture convention ticketing solution ) often support session check-in scanning or integration with mobile apps that attendees use as programme guides. By tracking attendance per session, you can calculate the fill rate of each room (attendance as a percentage of capacity). Aiming for panels to be well-attended but not overpacked is key. Overcrowding leads to safety issues and turned-away fans, while under-filled panels indicate either niche interest or scheduling missteps. As a rule of thumb: Ready to Sell Tickets? Create professional event pages with built-in payment processing, marketing tools, and real-time analytics. Create Your Event Event Ticketing Software Panel Fill Rate (Capacity) Interpretation Programming Action Next Year < 20% full (mostly empty) Very low interest or poor timing Reevaluate topic or time; consider cutting 20–60% full (moderate) Below potential Improve marketing or avoid content clashes 60–90% full (healthy) Good engagement Keep and refine; this hit the mark 90–100% full (popular) High demand, near capacity Strong interest; consider larger room Over capacity (overflow) Overwhelming demand Must address – bigger venue or repeat panel Tracking these metrics requires counting attendees diligently. At smaller cons, staff or volunteers can click counters at the door or collect tickets for limited-seating panels. Larger events rely on electronic check-in – for instance, using a mobile scanning app to scan badges or tickets at each session door. An all-in-one event platform like Ticket Fairy’s ticketing and analytics system can simplify this, as it logs entries and gives organisers a live attendance dashboard. Real-time data allows you to see if a room is filling up faster than expected and respond accordingly. (Some cons station crew at popular sessions with standby lines, opening overflow space or offering alternate viewing if data shows rooms near capacity.) The goal is to ensure you know exactly which panels fans are flocking to and which ones they skip. Real-Time Crowd Intelligence Flow — Tracking live attendance through badge scans helps you manage room capacities and respond to unexpected surges instantly. Harnessing Surveys and Fan Feedback Raw attendance numbers only tell part of the story. To truly program panels that resonate, you need qualitative insights from attendees. That’s where post-panel and post-convention surveys come in. Effective organisers collect attendee feedback on questions like: Which panels were your favourites? Which topics or guests would you like to see in the future? Did any sessions disappoint, and why? Combining this feedback with attendance data paints a fuller picture of panel performance. Many conventions deploy quick panel surveys via their mobile app or a QR code given out at the end of each session. Even a simple 1–5 star rating for each panel, plus an open comment field, can yield valuable pointers. For multi-track events, consider a short nightly survey during the con (when impressions are fresh) and a longer post-event survey afterward. Consistently, organisers find that response rates jump if you keep surveys short (5 questions or less) and perhaps incentivise them (e.g. a prize drawing for completed surveys). For example, a mid-sized sci-fi con in the UK saw survey response rates climb to 35% after offering a free signed poster to ten random respondents. Attendee surveys can reveal hidden gems and pain points that numbers alone might miss. You might discover that a panel with moderate attendance still earned rave reviews from those who went – hinting at a niche hit that could grow if promoted better. Or perhaps a well-attended panel received poor feedback due to content issues, which is crucial to know before you simply repeat it next year. One comprehensive industry report on event attendance notes that organisers who blend quantitative data (attendance, sales) with qualitative input (satisfaction scores, comments) get the clearest insight into event success . In short, listen to your fans. Their direct feedback, combined with hard data, is a powerful guide for curating next year’s schedule. Turn Fans Into Your Marketing Team Ticket Fairy's built-in referral rewards system incentivizes attendees to share your event, delivering 15-25% sales boosts and 30x ROI vs paid ads. Referral Marketing for Events Get Started Free Don’t overlook registration and demographic data as well. If your ticketing platform allows custom questions at checkout, consider asking attendees about their interests or fandoms. For instance, when buying badges, fans could tick which tracks (anime, comics, gaming, etc.) they’re most excited about. This pre-event data can hint at which content might draw crowds. An organiser of an Australian pop culture convention noticed a surge in attendees identifying as “cosplay enthusiasts” during registration, prompting the con to expand its cosplay programming and prop policy workshops. Sure enough, those sessions ended up standing-room-only. Modern platforms also capture data like what time tickets are bought or which marketing source brought an attendee – indirectly showing what announcements or guests drove interest. All these data points, from registration trends to panel ratings, feed into smarter programming decisions. Decoding Your Panel Fill Rates — Analyzing room occupancy percentages allows you to refine your content strategy and room assignments for future events. Analyzing the Data for Patterns and Preferences Collecting data is useless unless you analyze it for actionable insights. The next step in data-driven event programming is to sift through your attendance numbers, survey results, and other intel to spot trends. What patterns emerge from the data, and how can they inform your panel scheduling? Experienced con runners treat this analysis as a post-event ritual – a “programming post-mortem” that turns numbers into strategy. Grow Your Events Leverage referral marketing, social sharing incentives, and audience insights to sell more tickets. Sell Tickets Online Get Started Free Identifying Hot Topics and Underperformers Start by ranking your panels by attendance and by attendee satisfaction. Which sessions filled every seat, and which struggled to draw a crowd? Look for common threads among the top performers: Was it the theme (e.g., Marvel superhero panels outdrawing others), the format (Q&A sessions vs. lectures), or perhaps the star power of a guest? For example, at a large comic con in India, the organisers discovered that panels about new blockbuster film releases consistently had 80%+ fill rates, whereas classic comic lore panels averaged much lower. The takeaway was to increase content around upcoming movies and TV series – what’s hot now – to meet fan demand, while finding new hooks to boost classic content panels (like adding popular creators to those sessions). At the same time, identify underperforming panels. If certain topics repeatedly see <30% attendance, that’s a red flag. It could mean that content is too niche, or maybe the panel was scheduled against a big main event (and thus was doomed by conflict, not lack of interest). Data needs context: cross-reference the timing and room location for low-attendance sessions. You might find a scheduling clash or a far-flung room suppressed an otherwise worthy panel. For instance, one anime convention noticed all their academic lecture-style panels were poorly attended – not necessarily because attendees disliked the topics, but because those panels ran parallel to the cosplay contest and were located in a separate building. The next year, they adjusted the schedule to avoid that conflict and saw those panel attendance numbers double. It’s useful to categorise panels by type and genre when analysing. Break down your data by track, theme, and format. Maybe workshops and interactive panels had higher satisfaction scores than passive speaker panels – indicating fans crave more hands-on content. Or data might reveal that your gaming-related panels were 90% full while the science-fiction literature track lagged at 40% on average. These patterns help in reallocating emphasis. Many veteran organisers actually produce a simple report or heat map of their panel grid: highlighting which slots were most and least attended. This visualization can quickly show, for example, that Saturday mid-day sessions were jam-packed, while Sunday morning sessions (perhaps unsurprisingly) had sparse attendance. Informed by this, you might program lighter fare for early mornings and save blockbuster panels for peak times. Eliminating Content Clashes Forever — Sequencing related topics instead of scheduling them simultaneously ensures fans never have to choose between their favorite sessions. Beyond attendance figures, look at engagement metrics if available. Did certain panels generate a lot of social media buzz during the event? For example, if your event app or hashtag saw a spike in posts during the “Mystery Celebrity Panel” on Saturday, that’s a qualitative indicator of high interest. Likewise, if your panel feedback forms show that 95% of respondents “would recommend this panel to a friend,” that’s a session to consider expanding or repeating. According to IAEE’s industry data on conference metrics , participation is the single most important indicator of event success – people “vote with their feet” and their time. So dig into where attendees chose to spend their time. The patterns you find in that data are gold for future planning. Go Cashless With RFID Technology Enable contactless payments, faster entry, and real-time spending analytics with RFID wristbands and NFC-enabled ticketing for your events. RFID Cashless Event Technology Get Started Free Understanding Audience Segments and Interests Another powerful use of attendee data is identifying who your audience is and how different segments behave. Your convention is likely composed of various fan subgroups – for example, hardcore cosplayers, casual pop-culture fans, gamers, anime enthusiasts, etc. Data can help tailor programming to these segments. Start by examining any demographic info you have (age ranges, first-time vs. repeat attendees, VIP ticket holders vs. general) and see if their panel choices differ. For instance, repeat attendees might gravitate towards niche “insider” panels that go deeper into lore, while first-timers flock to celebrity Q&As and main attractions. A European gaming expo noticed that their attendees aged under 25 showed up in droves for esports tournament panels and game demo sessions, whereas those 25+ preferred developer talks and retro gaming discussions. By segmenting the feedback and attendance data, the organisers decided to create two new panel tracks the next year: one aimed at “pro gamers and esports fans” and another on “retro and industry topics” – effectively catering to both demographics more directly. Both tracks subsequently saw improved satisfaction scores as fans found content that spoke to them. If your ticketing or registration system integrates with a CRM or analytics tool, you can even overlay purchase behavior or marketing data onto programming preferences. For example, you might discover that attendees who bought VIP badges (or higher-priced tiers) are the ones filling the front rows of academic or niche panels – perhaps because they’re the super-fans with broader interests. Understanding these nuances allows for data-driven content curation: you can ensure each key audience segment has something tailored to them, and you market those sessions to the people most likely to be interested. Some advanced conventions experiment with attendee personas based on data. They cluster attendees into types (e.g. “The Cosplay Creator”, “The Collectibles Superfan”, “The Anime Binger”) and map out a sample itinerary of panels that each persona would love. Then they check if their schedule actually supports those ideal itineraries without conflict. This kind of analysis can highlight, say, that all the cosplay creator-oriented panels were bunched together, forcing a difficult choice, whereas they could be spread out. It’s an approach borrowed from corporate conferences, but it works for fan events too – ensuring your schedule offers a balanced journey for different interest groups. The more you understand your audience segments through data, the more precisely you can program content that each group will consider unmissable. Crafting Perfect Journeys for Every Fan — Designing schedules around specific attendee personas prevents interest conflicts and maximizes individual satisfaction. Scheduling Panels with Data-Driven Insights Collecting and analysing attendee data sets the stage – now it’s time to apply those insights to actually schedule your next convention’s panels. Data-driven scheduling means using evidence (not just gut instinct) to decide what panels to include, when and where to slot them, and how to manage them for maximum engagement. The result should be a programme that consistently draws full rooms and happy attendees. Here are key strategies to implement: Optimizing Room Allocation and Time Slots One of the most immediate payoffs of data is smarter room assignments. By predicting which panels will be most popular, you can match high-demand panels to larger rooms and lower-demand ones to smaller spaces. This sounds obvious, but without data it’s guesswork – many organisers have been caught off guard by a “sleeper hit” panel in too small a room or an overhyped session not filling a giant hall. Look at last year’s attendance and any pre-registration or interest indicators for new content. If a similar panel last year hit 95% capacity in a 500-seat room, consider moving it to a 800-seat room this time. Conversely, if an experimental panel only drew 50 people in a 400-seat hall, you might downsize that session or combine it with another topic. Smooth Entry With Mobile Check-In Scan tickets and manage entry with our mobile check-in app. Supports photo ID verification, real-time capacity tracking, and multi-gate coordination. Event Ticket Scanner App Get Started Data can help predict panel popularity surprisingly well. In fact, organizers of the PASS Summit tech conference used historical data and algorithms to forecast session attendance, successfully assigning rooms so that overcrowded sessions dropped from 17% of sessions to just 8% year-over-year . They analysed factors like speaker popularity and topic trends to make these predictions. For fan conventions, you can similarly weigh factors such as: the popularity of the franchise/topic, social media buzz, guest star draw, and previous attendance for similar panels. Even a simple ranking (e.g., “Tier 1” headliner panels, “Tier 2” mid-level interest, etc.) based on data can guide your room allocation. It’s far better to have a slightly too large room than to turn away hundreds at the door. As experienced organisers often say, empty seats don’t tweet angry complaints, but fans locked out of a full panel might. Aside from room size, use data to optimise time slotting. Your analysis might show certain time slots consistently outperform others. Is Saturday 11:00 AM a prime time when many fans are on site and energetic? Schedule a big-name panel or highly anticipated topic then. Perhaps your data shows that late afternoon sessions dip in attendance – that might be a good time for niche topics or secondary content, since fewer will attend anything then. Also consider patterns like meal times and other activities: for example, if a major cosplay contest or concert is at 7 PM, any panel scheduled opposite it could suffer. Stagger your “marquee” events so they don’t cannibalise each other’s audiences. A data-driven grid might entail anchoring each day with one or two tentpole panels (based on prior popularity) and filling around them with complementary content. Another scheduling tweak informed by data is repeating popular sessions. If you have a panel that always fills up and still has excess demand, consider running it twice (maybe once each on two different days) or offering an encore on the final day. Some conventions do this with extremely high-demand content – for instance, a Japanese culture panel in New York might run on both Saturday and Sunday if the first session maxed out. Data from prior days (or previous years) can justify these encores. It’s a way to spread out attendance and give more fans a chance to see the content they want. Just be mindful to schedule repeats such that they don’t conflict with related content that the same audience would also want. Avoiding Conflicts and Managing Crowds Your attendee data is also a map of fan interests, which can help you avoid scheduling conflicts that split your audience. A classic rookie mistake in programming is to schedule two super-popular panels at the same time, forcing fans to choose and leaving both half-full rather than one completely full. Data can prevent this. By reviewing which panels appealed to similar attendee segments (from surveys or pass scans), you can identify potential conflicts. For instance, if you know the attendees who went to the “Game of Thrones Fan Discussion” also largely attended the “Lord of the Rings panel” last year, don’t put those in the same time block this year – you likely have a significant overlap in audience. Instead, schedule them sequentially or at least far apart. Using data in this way can increase overall panel attendance by ensuring fans aren’t forced to skip one favourite for another. Transforming Registration Data Into Content — Using pre-event interest surveys ensures your programming schedule matches the specific fandoms attending your show. Many large cons also adopt tools like a panel reservation system or “lottery” for the most in-demand sessions. This not only improves fan satisfaction by making access fair, but it gives organisers excellent data on interest levels. For example, SXSW’s PanelPicker system allows the community to vote on proposed sessions ahead of the event, directly telling organisers which topics have the most fan support. Fan conventions might use a simpler approach: during registration or via the event app, allow attendees to mark a few panels they’re most interested in (not as a guarantee, just as a gauge or RSVP). If 2,000 attendees pre-favourited a panel that only seats 500, you know to expect long lines or implement a ticketing mechanism for that panel. New York Comic Con, for instance, has used online lotteries for popular panels in limited rooms – the data from those sign-ups helps them anticipate crowd size and allocate security and line space accordingly. Embracing these tools, especially if your convention ticketing platform supports session reservations, turns potential crowd control headaches into manageable, data-informed logistics. Even with great scheduling, the reality is some panels will be very popular. That’s where data-informed crowd management comes in. Monitor attendance data during the event (many platforms offer real-time dashboards) to see if certain sessions are over capacity or lines are forming hours early. Armed with these insights, you can deploy solutions on the fly. For example, Comic-Con International’s Hall H uses a wristband system to manage overnight queues , ensuring only the first 6,500 in line (Hall H’s capacity) stay in queue. While not every event has Hall H levels of hype, the principle stands: use info on demand to implement fair access. Perhaps you designate an overflow room with a live video feed for a panel that’s blowing up – data from past days or pre-signups can justify having that backup. Or you adjust room assignments for Day 2 if Day 1 data showed you underestimated an audience. Some cons even re-run a “surprise hit” panel on the final afternoon once they see how beloved it was. Free Tool: Split Tickets for Max Gross Given capacity and a target price, the optimizer proposes Early Bird / GA / VIP allocations and prices — with projected gross at 100%, 80% and 60% sell-through. Tier Allocation Optimizer See All Free Tools It’s also worth planning for line management and entry order using data about who has access. Many premium ticket holders (VIPs, etc.) expect early entry to big panels. Data can tell you what portion of a room might be taken by VIPs versus general attendees, which helps plan separate queues or reserved seating blocks. In short, a data-driven mindset doesn’t stop at scheduling – it extends to how you execute the seating and flow. (For further reading on avoiding queue chaos, see our guide on advanced convention crowd management tactics that keep lines orderly while maximizing fan satisfaction.) By anticipating needs and conflicts through data, you ensure that full rooms are a positive – an electric atmosphere – rather than a negative experience. Case Studies: Data in Action at Fan Conventions Nothing illustrates the impact of attendee data better than real-world examples. Here are a few cases from conventions globally that have leveraged data to boost panel success: SXSW (Austin, USA) – Community Voting Shapes the Schedule: One of the most well-known examples of data-driven programming is South by Southwest’s PanelPicker® process. SXSW invites its community to vote on proposed sessions months in advance , effectively crowd-sourcing data on what content attendees most want to see. Organisers combine this fan input (which can total tens of thousands of votes) with internal curation. The result is a conference lineup that consistently matches attendee interests – because it was literally shaped by would-be attendees. For SXSW, this process has helped keep session rooms packed year after year; when fans have a voice in programming, they show up for those sessions. Convention organisers can take a page from SXSW by involving fans in programming decisions, whether via pre-con polls or advisory committees, to ensure the content resonates. It’s data-driven scheduling in the form of direct democracy. Anime Expo (Los Angeles, USA) – Refining Content via Surveys: Anime Expo (AX), North America’s largest anime convention, gathers extensive attendee feedback to fine-tune its programming. After AX 2022, organisers noticed through surveys and panel attendance data that interest in industry insider panels (like discussions with anime producers and studios) was surging. In response, AX 2023 expanded that track with more sessions and larger rooms. They featured panels by major Japanese anime studios in the convention’s Petree Hall, which seats thousands. The outcome was phenomenal – those panels hit full capacity with lines out the door, and post-con surveys rated the industry track one of the year’s best additions. By contrast, AX also saw that some fan-run community panels had dipped in attendance. Rather than cutting them blindly, organisers cross-referenced feedback and discovered that scheduling was the culprit: many fan panels were slotted early morning when attendees were either in line for big events or simply not yet on-site. With that insight, AX 2024 shifted many fan-run panels to early afternoon slots and saw participation rebound strongly. This example shows how combining attendance stats with direct fan feedback allows a convention to pivot programming strategy and reap immediate results in attendance. Capturing the Voice of the Fan — Combining star ratings with direct feedback reveals the true sentiment and quality behind the raw attendance numbers. MidSizeCon (Global Examples) – Predictive Room Allocation: A mid-sized gaming convention in Germany (let’s call it MidSizeCon) faced complaints in 2022 about overcrowded and half-empty panels – sometimes both on the same day. For 2023, the organisers harnessed their data to predict and allocate better. They noticed that every time they had a panel about “Retro Gaming Classics,” it drew a consistent 300+ people, despite being in a 200-seat room previously. Meanwhile, a series of “Indie Game Dev” panels were in a 500-seat theatre but only ever saw about 150 attendees on average. So MidSizeCon flipped their approach: they upgraded the retro gaming panel to the bigger room and moved the indie dev talks to a smaller one, aligning capacity with demonstrated demand. They also looked at time-of-day patterns – data showed that the retro panel drew even bigger crowds when scheduled right after lunch, so they gave it a prime early afternoon slot. The results were clear on site: no more turned-away fans for the retro session (the larger room accommodated everyone), and the indie sessions felt nicely full in the smaller space, creating better energy. Attendance for both tracks improved, and feedback was positive across the board. This case underlines that even without fancy algorithms, basic data analysis (past headcounts and time slot successes) can dramatically improve room utilisation and audience experience. Professional Conferences – Lessons for Fan Cons: It’s worth noting that corporate conferences and trade shows have been employing data-driven session scheduling for years, and fan conventions are now catching up. For instance, a tech conference used machine learning on its attendee data to anticipate interest levels , reducing overflow incidents significantly. They found that speaker popularity was a top predictor of attendance – a finding that resonates in fan events too (a famous actor or creator will spike numbers regardless of panel topic). Many such conferences also correlate session rating with attendance and sometimes find surprising results, like how a packed room doesn’t guarantee high session quality ratings . Fan convention organisers similarly should balance popularity with quality – data can flag situations where a panel drew a crowd but got poor feedback, indicating a need to improve content or moderation next time. The crossover lesson is clear: more data leads to better programming decisions, whether for industry keynotes or cosplay sketch workshops. Collect Any Attendee Data at Checkout Add custom registration fields to your checkout — dietary needs, t-shirt sizes, company names, and more. Conditional logic and per-ticket-type fields. Custom Event Registration Fields Get Started Free Each of these examples – from letting fans vote, to analysing surveys, to reallocating rooms – shows data’s tangible impact. Conventions that take a data-driven approach tend to see higher overall panel attendance and attendee satisfaction. Fans feel their interests are heard and met. When you program based on what the data says your attendees crave, you create a virtuous cycle: successful panels generate excitement, which drives word-of-mouth and higher attendance the next year. It’s no surprise that events known for great programming often have robust data practices behind the scenes. Continuous Improvement: Building a Year-Round Data Feedback Loop The final piece of a data-driven programming strategy is making it continuous and iterative. The goal is not just to use attendee data for one event, but to build a feedback loop that makes each year’s convention better than the last. Veteran organisers treat data like a compass – guiding decisions not only in scheduling panels, but in marketing, ticketing, and overall event design. Here’s how to embed data into your year-round planning cycle: Managing Blockbuster Panel Demand — Implementing overflow rooms and fair access systems turns high-demand sessions into smooth, professional experiences for everyone. Post-Event Analysis and Debrief: Right after your convention, do a thorough data review while everything is fresh. Generate reports from your ticketing system and registration platform with the panel attendance numbers, no-show rates for special events, and any other stats (e.g. how many people used the panel reservation system if you had one). Combine this with your survey summaries and team observations. Many teams hold a post-con “brain dump” meeting where department heads (programming, guest relations, operations) share impressions – backing those up with data prevents decisions from relying purely on anecdotal memories. For instance, instead of “Saturday felt really busy,” you can say “ Saturday 1-3 PM saw 20% higher panel attendance than any other period , possibly due to the two blockbuster panels – next year let’s space those out.” Document these insights in a programming playbook for the next edition. Set Data-Backed Goals for Next Year: Use insights to establish concrete goals. Maybe you want to improve average panel fill rate from 60% to 75%, or reduce the number of panels under 20% capacity to zero. You might aim for a certain uplift in satisfaction scores for panels, or to eliminate complaints about panel schedule conflicts. Having measurable objectives helps focus your strategy. For example, if feedback showed confusion about overlapping big panels, a goal could be “zero overlapping Tier-1 panels” in the schedule. If panel attendance on Sunday dipped to 50% of Saturday’s, a goal might be “increase Sunday panel attendance by 25%” – achieved by scheduling a must-see event Sunday morning or offering an incentive for fans to stick around. By tying goals to data, you can later quantify if your new programming strategy worked. Implementing Changes with the Right Tools: Achieving data-driven improvements often requires the right tools. Modern event management platforms can be invaluable here. Ideally, you want a system that integrates ticketing, scheduling, and analytics so that all your attendee data is in one place. Using a solution like Ticket Fairy’s all-in-one platform gives organisers 100% ownership of their attendee data – meaning you can export and analyse every click and scan. Data portability is vital; you don’t want your insights locked behind a vendor. Ensure any platform you evaluate lets you easily access raw data (sales, check-ins, survey responses) for your own analysis. Also look for features like real-time dashboards (to monitor at-event trends) and CRM integration to enrich profiles of attendees with their panel interests . A great tool will not make decisions for you, but it will surface the information you need when planning your schedule. Additionally, technology can help execute some data-driven tactics effortlessly. For example, Ticket Fairy’s system includes referral tracking and promo codes, which lets you see which announcements or guests spurred ticket sales. If a particular panel announcement (say, a special reunion panel) led to a spike in referrals and new registrations, that’s data you can use to allocate more time or marketing to similar content. On the operations side, robust ticketing platforms offer access control apps – you can use these not just at the main entrance, but at panel rooms to scan badges for entry. All those scans feed back into your analytics to show live attendance numbers by room. Some events incorporate RFID wristbands for seamless tracking across the venue. When evaluating solutions, consider one that has these advanced capabilities without sacrificing attendee experience. Fans shouldn’t feel like they’re being tracked – it should be smooth and in service of a better event for them. Mastering Strategic Room Allocation — Matching session popularity with the right-sized venue creates a better atmosphere and prevents fan frustration from lockouts. Marketing the Improved Experience: As you implement data-driven changes, let your attendees know that you heard them. For example, if surveys complained about long lines for a popular panel, you might announce “New for next year: a reservation system for the most popular panels to guarantee your seat.” This not only addresses a pain point but becomes a marketing asset to drive early ticket sales. Many organisers launch referral programs (turning fans into ambassadors) to boost attendance once they’ve crafted a compelling schedule. After all, a well-programmed con is easier to promote – fans will be excited about the content. A referral initiative can amplify this, and data helps here too. You can track which fan ambassadors bring in attendees for particular segments. For instance, if an influencer in the anime community sells many referral tickets, perhaps their followers will want more anime panels – data you gather as registrations roll in can validate that and you could still adjust your final schedule accordingly. Finally, stay agile and iterate. The fan landscape evolves constantly – what was a hit panel this year might cool off by next year as new shows, games, or memes capture fandom’s imagination. By keeping a year-round pulse on fan discussions (online forums, social media trends, etc.) and comparing with your own attendee data, you won’t be caught flat-footed. Many conventions now maintain a community presence year-round (via Discord servers, fan clubs, etc.) where they can poll their core audience on potential panel ideas. Coupled with solid post-event analytics, this ensures when it’s programming time, you’re armed with up-to-date insight on what will draw a crowd. It’s this continuous feedback loop – plan, execute, measure, adjust – that turns data from a one-time helper into a permanent compass for your convention’s growth. In summary, building attendee data into your panel programming cycle transforms the process from educated guesswork into a science-backed art. It doesn’t replace the need for creative vision or understanding of your fandom – rather, it enhances it with evidence. The conventions that thrive in today’s competitive scene are those that treat data as a friend of creativity, not its enemy. Use the numbers to empower your team’s passion and intuition, and you’ll create an event schedule that not only fills seats, but leaves fans counting days until they return. Frequently Asked Questions What is a good panel fill rate for a convention? A healthy panel fill rate for a convention is between 60% and 90% of the room’s capacity. This level indicates strong audience engagement without causing safety issues or turning fans away. Panels falling below 20% capacity usually require reevaluating the topic, while those exceeding 100% need larger venues. How do convention organizers track panel attendance? Convention organizers track panel attendance using technology like badge scanning, RFID tracking at room entrances, and mobile app check-ins. These digital systems provide precise, real-time headcounts and individual attendee preferences, replacing manual click counters and allowing staff to monitor if rooms are filling up faster than expected. Why is data-driven panel scheduling important for fan conventions? Data-driven panel scheduling ensures programming aligns directly with fan demand, leading to packed rooms and higher attendee satisfaction. Leveraging attendance metrics and surveys helps organizers allocate popular topics to larger rooms, avoid scheduling misfires, and boost overall event economics through increased on-site spending and happier sponsors. How can event organizers avoid scheduling conflicts for convention panels? Organizers avoid scheduling conflicts by analyzing attendee data to identify overlapping fan interests and separating those panels into different time blocks. By reviewing past attendance and survey data, planners can ensure two highly popular sessions targeting the same audience segment do not run simultaneously, maximizing overall participation. How does attendee demographic data improve event programming? Attendee demographic data improves event programming by revealing specific content preferences among different audience segments. Analyzing factors like age, ticket tiers, and registration interests allows organizers to tailor panel tracks directly to distinct groups, such as creating dedicated esports sessions for younger attendees or deep-lore panels for VIPs. How do large conventions manage crowds for highly popular panels? Large conventions manage crowds for popular panels by utilizing advance reservation systems, online lotteries, and real-time attendance dashboards. Organizers also deploy on-the-fly solutions like opening overflow rooms with live video feeds or issuing wristbands to cap queues, ensuring fair access and safe line management for high-demand sessions. What is the best way to collect attendee feedback on convention panels? The best way to collect attendee feedback is through short, incentivized post-panel surveys deployed via mobile apps or QR codes. Keeping surveys under five questions and offering rewards, like prize drawings, significantly boosts response rates, providing qualitative insights that raw attendance numbers cannot reveal. How do community voting systems influence convention panel schedules? Community voting systems influence panel schedules by crowdsourcing direct fan input on proposed sessions months before the event. Platforms like SXSW’s PanelPicker allow organizers to combine thousands of attendee votes with internal curation, ensuring the final lineup matches actual audience interests and guarantees packed rooms.

body_text: We've added two new roles to the PropelAuth dashboard: Developer and Customer Management . The idea behind both is the same: give people access to everything they need for their job, without access to anything extra. In practice, the person setting up your login methods and the person helping a customer fix their SSO connection are doing pretty different things. Before today, you'd have had to give both of them broader access than either actually needed. These roles fix that. Developer # The Developer role is for engineers who need to configure how the project works. That covers updating signup and login settings, managing organization settings, configuring API keys, setting up integrations, updating roles and permissions, configuring MCP and OAuth, setting custom domains, and generating backend API keys. Developers can view users and organizations, but can't create, modify, or delete them. It's the right fit for someone who needs full access to the configuration side but shouldn't be touching customer data. Customer Management # The Customer Management role is for support and ops teams who work with users and organizations directly. That includes creating and deleting accounts, blocking and unblocking users, managing Enterprise SSO and SCIM connections, changing role mappings, managing org membership, and archiving API keys. It doesn't include any access to project configuration, so your support team can do their job without being able to accidentally change your login settings. How these fit with the existing roles # Nothing changes for existing roles. Owner, Admin, Member, and ReadOnly all work the same way they did before, and you now have six to choose from: Owner : Full access Admin : Full access except billing, impersonation settings, and org membership settings Developer : Project configuration only; no user or org management (new) Customer Management : User and org management only; no project configuration (new) Member : Moderate access across both areas ReadOnly : View-only Neither new role can manage teammates or update billing. That stays with Owner and Admin. Full permission breakdown # Permission Developer Customer Management Users View users ✓ ✓ Create / modify users — ✓ Block / unblock users — ✓ Delete users — ✓ Organizations View organizations ✓ ✓ Create / manage orgs — ✓ Enable Enterprise SSO / SCIM — ✓ Delete organizations — ✓ Project configuration Update signup / login settings ✓ — Manage API key settings ✓ — Configure MCP / OAuth / integrations ✓ — Update roles & permissions ✓ — Team & billing Invite / manage teammates — — Update billing — — For the full matrix across all six roles, check out the docs . The roles are live for all accounts now. To assign them, head to your organization settings in the dashboard.

title: How 3D Printing Is Transforming Medical Tool and Equipment Production
summary: Learn how 3D-printed medical tools help teams create custom instruments, guides, and equipment for faster healthcare innovation and better outcomes.
body_text: 3D-printed medical tools can often be produced in days instead of weeks, allowing engineers to build parts on demand, refine designs quickly, and move into evaluation faster. That is helping healthcare teams develop more adaptable solutions, with equipment built for a specific patient or procedure. Learn more about medical manufacturing solutions from Protolabs. What Are 3D-Printed Medical Tools? 3D-printed medical tools are instruments, guides, fixtures, and support equipment made with additive manufacturing. That can include surgical instruments, patient-specific guides, prototypes, and custom hospital equipment. Engineers designing medical devices often rely on four 3D printing processes: stereolithography (SLA) , selective laser sintering (SLS) , Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) , and direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) . The best fit usually comes down to the application, material requirements, and production goals. That decision is important because medical parts typically need to meet tighter criteria than general prototypes, especially around sterilization, biocompatibility, and consistent performance. Protolabs offers medical 3D printing services for teams that need to meet those demands while moving quickly from design to part. Materials for 3D-Printed Medical Tools Material selection for 3D-printed medical tools depends on how the part will be used, cleaned, and handled. The processes below cover the most relevant printable options, ranging from durable polymers to high-strength metals, each with different trade-offs for biocompatibility, sterilization tolerance, and structural performance. Process Medically relevant materials Best for Tolerances Stereolithography (SLA) Polycarbonate Silicone Fine detail, smooth surfaces, and concept models or guides ±0.002 in. (±0.05mm) Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) Nylon TPU Durable plastic parts, and complex geometries, and functional prototypes ±0.010 in. (±0.25mm) Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) Nylon Strong plastic parts, repeatable builds, and end-use components ±0.012 in. (±0.30mm) Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) Titanium Stainless Steel Cobalt Chrome High-strength metal tools and demanding medical applications ±0.003 in. (±0.076mm) Key Applications for 3D-Printed Medical Tools 3D printing is especially useful for medical tools that need to be customized, produced quickly, or shaped in ways traditional methods cannot easily handle. Surgical instruments: During surgery, doctors need instruments that feel steady, precise, and comfortable in their hands. 3D printing helps teams test new geometries faster and create instruments like forceps, clamps, and retractors that are tailored to a specific procedure or surgeon's preference. Patient-specific surgical guides: No two patients are exactly alike, and 3D printing makes it easier to produce custom guides that support more precise placement, alignment, and surgical approach. Custom fixtures and hospital equipment: 3D printing can help hospitals, labs, and medical device teams quickly manufacture small functional parts that are too specialized for mass production, such as holders, positioning aids, test fixtures, or replacement components. Why Use 3D Printing for These Applications? 3D printing gives teams more room to solve the actual problem instead of designing around manufacturing constraints. Here is where 3D-printed medical tools often deliver the most value: Design freedom: Internal channels, ergonomic curves, and other complex shapes can come out of a single build instead of requiring difficult machining or molds. Per-patient customization: 3D printing makes it easier to create custom guides and other tools that directly match a patient's anatomical needs. Fast production without tooling or molds: Parts can move from computer-aided design (CAD) file to finished tool in a matter of days, which is essential when a surgery is scheduled or a validation run is holding up a launch. Improved ergonomics: Small changes to grip, balance, or weight can make medical tools easier to control during long or delicate procedures. Emerging and Future Opportunities Medical tool development is changing fast, and 3D printing is helping drive the innovations. Digital surgical planning: CT-to-CAD-to-print workflows are making it easier to turn patient imaging into anatomy-specific cutting guides, drill guides, and procedure planning models before a surgery even begins. Advanced metal printing: Better metal printing and post-processing are facilitating lighter tools, more intricate geometries, and stronger custom components. Similar advances are also showing up in implants such as porous titanium structures that can support bone growth in to the surface over time. Distributed manufacturing: On-demand printing through networks like Protolabs Network brings specialized medical tools within reach of healthcare settings that previously can't access them. For a broader view, check out the recent 3D printing trends in the medical industry. Challenges and Considerations of 3D Printing in Healthcare 3D printing is powerful, but engineers still need to plan around the realities of medical manufacturing. Regulatory requirements: Medical applications may require strict documentation, validation, and compliance planning. Material limitations: Not every printable material is suitable for sterilization, skin contact, or demanding clinical use. For high-temperature or implant-grade needs, parts may need to be machined or molded rather than printed. Quality control: Production use depends on documented process parameters, post-processing validation, and inspection workflows that hold across every build, particularly for regulated devices. Production economics: 3D printing is great for low volumes and high-mix funs, but once quantities hit thoughts of identical parts, injection molding or machining often have lower per-unit costs. The Bigger Impact 3D printed medical tools are giving teams a faster, more flexible way to develop equipment for specific procedures, patients, and clinical needs. In both advanced and resource-limited healthcare settings, that agility opens the door to an ever-expanding range of practical, patient-centered solutions. Frequently Asked Questions Can 3D-printed tools be sterilized? expand_less expand_more Yes. Many medical-grade polymers and metals can tolerate autoclave , gamma, or ethylene oxide (EtO) sterilization, though compatibility depends on the material and process. What materials are used for 3D-printed surgical tools? expand_less expand_more Common options include titanium and stainless steel for reusable instruments, along with nylon and photopolymer resins for guides and single-use tools. body_text: Back to Blog 3 MIN READ Memorial Day weekend marks the unofficial start of summer — and one of the busiest travel periods of the year. With millions of drivers hitting the road, gas stations and food marts become essential pit stops. High traffic means high opportunity, but it also means higher energy consumption, longer operating hours, and more pressure on your equipment. The good news: a few smart energy moves can keep your site efficient, comfortable, and profitable during the holiday surge. Optimize Your Refrigeration Before the Crowds Arrive Refrigeration is one of the biggest energy drains in a convenience store, especially when customers are constantly opening cooler doors. Check door seals — A loose or cracked gasket can waste hundreds of dollars in cold air loss. Pre-cool your units — Lower temperatures slightly the night before peak traffic so units don’t struggle to recover. Stock efficiently — Avoid overpacking shelves, which restricts airflow and forces compressors to work harder. A well-tuned cooler keeps drinks cold and customers happy without spiking your energy bill. Use Smart Lighting to Handle Extended Hours Lighting can account for up to 40% of a gas station’s energy use during busy weekends. Switch to LEDs — They use up to 75% less energy and last longer. Install motion sensors in low-traffic areas like storage rooms and back offices. Adjust canopy lighting schedules — Bright enough for safety, but not wasteful. Good lighting boosts visibility, safety, and curb appeal — all essential when travelers are choosing where to stop. Keep HVAC Running Efficiently in High-Traffic Conditions With doors opening constantly, your HVAC system works overtime. Replace or clean filters before the holiday weekend. Use smart thermostats to maintain consistent temperatures. Seal gaps around doors to reduce cool-air loss. A comfortable store encourages customers to linger — and buy more. Manage Fuel Pump Energy Use Fuel pumps run continuously, but you can still reduce waste. Check pump canopy sensors to ensure lights aren’t running during daylight. Inspect pump air compressors for leaks that cause unnecessary cycling. Use energy-efficient pump lighting to cut overnight costs. Small improvements add up fast when pumps run 24/7. Prepare Your Ice Machines and Freezers for Heavy Demand Ice is one of the top-selling items during Memorial Day weekend — and one of the biggest energy hogs. Clean condenser coils to improve efficiency. Empty and sanitize bins so machines don’t overwork. Pre-produce ice during off-peak hours when electricity rates may be lower. A reliable ice supply keeps customers happy and boosts impulse sales. Train Staff on Quick Energy Wins Your team is your first line of defense against energy waste. Teach simple shutdown routines for equipment not needed during peak hours. Assign cooler-door checks to prevent propping or unnecessary openings. Encourage fast restocking to minimize open-door time. A few minutes of training can save hours of wasted energy. Use Data to Predict and Prepare for Peak Times If your POS or fuel system tracks traffic patterns, use that data. Identify peak hours and pre-cool or pre-stock accordingly. Adjust staffing to reduce bottlenecks and keep doors closed more often. Monitor energy spikes to catch equipment issues early. Data-driven prep keeps your site running smoothly even when the parking lot is packed. Promote Your Energy-Smart Upgrades to Travelers Customers love knowing they’re supporting a business that’s efficient and environmentally conscious. Highlight LED upgrades on signage. Advertise efficient refrigeration as part of your “coldest drinks in town” message. Share sustainability efforts on social media. Energy efficiency isn’t just cost-saving — it’s a marketing advantage. Final Takeaway Memorial Day weekend is a massive opportunity for gas stations and food marts. With smart energy practices, you can handle the surge, reduce operational stress, and keep your energy costs under control — all while delivering a better experience for travelers. with previously treated, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic, well-differentiated extra-pancreatic NET. CABOMETYX tablets have also received regulatory approvals in over 65 countries outside the U.S. and Japan, including the EU. In 2016, Exelixis granted Ipsen Pharma SAS exclusive rights for the commercialization and further clinical development of cabozantinib outside of the U.S. and Japan. In 2017, Exelixis granted exclusive rights to Takeda Pharmaceutical Company Limited for the commercialization and further clinical development of cabozantinib for all future indications in Japan. Exelixis holds the exclusive rights to develop and commercialize cabozantinib in the U.S. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Hemorrhage: CABOMETYX can cause severe and fatal hemorrhages. The incidence of Grade 3-5 hemorrhagic events was 5% in CABOMETYX patients in RCC, HCC, and DTC studies. Discontinue CABOMETYX for Grade 3-4 hemorrhage and before surgery. Do not administer to patients who have a recent history of hemorrhage, including hemoptysis, hematemesis, or melena. Perforations and Fistulas: Fistulas, including fatal cases, and gastrointestinal (GI) perforations, including fatal cases, each occurred in 1% of CABOMETYX patients. Monitor for signs and symptoms, and discontinue CABOMETYX in patients with Grade 4 fistulas or GI perforation. Thromboembolic Events: CABOMETYX can cause arterial or venous thromboembolic events. Venous thromboembolism occurred in 7% (including 4% pulmonary embolism) and arterial thromboembolism in 2% of CABOMETYX patients. Fatal thrombotic events have occurred. Discontinue CABOMETYX in patients who develop an acute myocardial infarction or serious arterial or venous thromboembolic events. Hypertension and Hypertensive Crisis: CABOMETYX can cause hypertension, including hypertensive crisis. Hypertension was reported in 37% (16% Grade 3 and <1% Grade 4) of CABOMETYX patients. In CABINET (n=195), hypertension occurred in 65% (26% Grade 3) of CABOMETYX patients. Do not initiate CABOMETYX in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. Monitor blood pressure regularly during CABOMETYX treatment. Withhold CABOMETYX for hypertension that is not adequately controlled; when controlled, resume at a reduced dose. Permanently discontinue CABOMETYX for severe hypertension that cannot be controlled with antihypertensive therapy or for hypertensive crisis. Cardiac Failure: CABOMETYX can cause severe and fatal cardiac failure. Cardiac failure occurred in 0.5% of patients treated with CABOMETYX as a single agent, including fatal cardiac failure in 0.1% of patients. Consider baseline and periodic evaluations of left ventricular ejection fraction. Monitor for signs and symptoms of cardiovascular events. Withhold and resume at a reduced dose upon recovery or permanently discontinue depending on the severity. Diarrhea: CABOMETYX can cause diarrhea and it occurred in 62% (10% Grade 3) of treated patients. Monitor and manage patients using antidiarrheals as indicated. Withhold CABOMETYX until improvement to ≤ Grade 1; resume at a reduced dose. Palmar-Plantar Erythrodysesthesia (PPE): CABOMETYX can cause PPE and it occurred in 45% of treated patients (13% Grade 3). Withhold CABOMETYX until PPE resolves or decreases to Grade 1 and resume at a reduced dose for intolerable Grade 2 PPE or Grade 3 PPE. Hepatotoxicity: CABOMETYX in combination with nivolumab in RCC can cause hepatic toxicity with higher frequencies of Grades 3 and 4 ALT and AST elevations compared to CABOMETYX alone. With the combination of CABOMETYX and nivolumab, Grades 3 and 4 increased ALT or AST were seen in 11% of patients. Monitor liver enzymes before initiation of treatment and periodically. Consider more frequent monitoring as compared to when the drugs are administered as single agents. Consider withholding CABOMETYX and/or nivolumab, initiating corticosteroid therapy, and/or permanently discontinuing the combination for severe or life-threatening hepatotoxicity. Adrenal Insufficiency: CABOMETYX in combination with nivolumab can cause primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal insufficiency occurred in 4.7% (15/320) of patients with RCC who received CABOMETYX with nivolumab, including Grade 3 (2.2%), and Grade 2 (1.9%) adverse reactions. Withhold CABOMETYX and/or nivolumab and resume CABOMETYX at a reduced dose depending on severity. Proteinuria: Proteinuria was observed in 8% of CABOMETYX patients. Monitor urine protein regularly during CABOMETYX treatment. For Grade 2 or 3 proteinuria, withhold CABOMETYX until improvement to ≤ Grade 1 proteinuria; resume CABOMETYX at a reduced dose. Discontinue CABOMETYX in patients who develop nephrotic syndrome. Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (ONJ): CABOMETYX can cause ONJ and it occurred in <1% of treated patients. Perform an oral examination prior to CABOMETYX initiation and periodically during treatment. Advise patients regarding good oral hygiene practices. Withhold CABOMETYX for at least 3 weeks prior to scheduled dental surgery or invasive dental procedures. Withhold CABOMETYX for development of ONJ until complete resolution; resume at a reduced dose. Impaired Wound Healing: CABOMETYX can cause impaired wound healing. Withhold CABOMETYX for at least 3 weeks prior to elective surgery. Do not administer for at least 2 weeks after major surgery and until adequate wound healing. The safety of resumption of CABOMETYX after resolution of wound healing complications has not been established. Reversible Posterior Leukoencephalopathy Syndrome (RPLS): CABOMETYX can cause RPLS. Perform evaluation for RPLS and diagnose by characteristic finding on MRI any patient presenting with seizures, headache, visual disturbances, confusion, or altered mental function. Discontinue CABOMETYX in patients who develop RPLS. Thyroid Dysfunction: CABOMETYX can cause thyroid dysfunction, primarily hypothyroidism, and it occurred in 19% of treated patients (0.4% Grade 3). Assess for signs of thyroid dysfunction prior to the initiation of CABOMETYX and monitor for signs and symptoms during treatment. Hypocalcemia: CABOMETYX can cause hypocalcemia, with the highest incidence in DTC patients. Based on the safety population, hypocalcemia occurred in 13% of CABOMETYX patients (2% Grade 3 and 1% Grade 4). Monitor blood calcium levels and replace calcium as necessary during treatment. Withhold and resume CABOMETYX at a reduced dose upon recovery or permanently discontinue CABOMETYX depending on severity. Embryo-Fetal Toxicity: CABOMETYX can cause fetal harm. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk to a fetus and advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with CABOMETYX and for 4 months after the last dose. ADVERSE REACTIONS The most common (≥20%) adverse reactions are: CABOMETYX as a single agent: diarrhea, fatigue, PPE, decreased appetite, hypertension, nausea, vomiting, weight decreased, and constipation. CABOMETYX in combination with nivolumab: diarrhea, fatigue, hepatotoxicity, PPE, stomatitis, rash, hypertension, hypothyroidism, musculoskeletal pain, decreased appetite, nausea, dysgeusia, abdominal pain, cough, and upper respiratory tract infection. DRUG INTERACTIONS Strong CYP3A4 Inhibitors: If coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors cannot be avoided, reduce the CABOMETYX dosage. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice. Strong or Moderate CYP3A4 Inducers: If coadministration with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers cannot be avoided, increase the CABOMETYX dosage. Avoid St. John’s wort. USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS Lactation: Advise women not to breastfeed during CABOMETYX treatment and for 4 months after the final dose. Hepatic Impairment: In patients with moderate hepatic impairment, reduce the CABOMETYX dosage. Avoid CABOMETYX in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Pediatric Use: Physeal widening has been observed in children with open growth plates when treated with CABOMETYX. Physeal and longitudinal growth monitoring is recommended in children (12 years and older) with open growth plates. Consider interrupting or discontinuing CABOMETYX if abnormalities occur. The safety and effectiveness of CABOMETYX in pediatric patients less than 12 years of age have not been established. Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information https://www.cabometyx.com/downloads/CABOMETYXUSPI.pdf . You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.FDA.gov/medwatch or call 1-800-FDA-1088. About Zanzalintinib Zanzalintinib is a novel oral kinase inhibitor that inhibits the activity of the TAM kinases (TYRO3, AXL, MER), MET and VEGF receptors. These kinases play important roles in oncogenic processes, including tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, angiogenesis, drug resistance and evasion of antitumor immunity. The zanzalintinib development program includes a series of ongoing and planned pivotal trials to explore its therapeutic potential in CRC, clear cell and non-clear cell RCC, and NET, as well as earlier-stage trials in meningioma, lung cancer and castration-resistant prostate cancer. In February 2026, Exelixis announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) accepted the company’s New Drug Application for zanzalintinib, in combination with atezolizumab (Tecentriq®), for the treatment of adult patients with mCRC who have been previously treated with fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin- and irinotecan-based chemotherapy, and, if RAS wild-type, an anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) therapy. The FDA assigned a Prescription Drug User Fee Act target action date of December 3, 2026. Zanzalintinib is an investigational agent that is not approved for any use and is the subject of ongoing clinical trials. About Exelixis Exelixis is a globally ambitious oncology company innovating next-generation medicines and regimens at the forefront of cancer care. Powered by drug discovery and development excellence, we are rapidly evolving our product portfolio to target an expanding range of tumor types and indications with our clinically differentiated pipeline of small molecules and biotherapeutics. This comprehensive approach harnesses decades of robust investment in our science and partnerships to advance our pipeline of franchise molecules, including our novel oral kinase inhibitor zanzalintinib, and to extend the impact of our flagship commercial product, CABOMETYX® (cabozantinib). Exelixis is driven by a bold scientific pursuit to create transformational treatments that give more patients hope for the future. For information about the company and its mission to help cancer patients recover stronger and live longer, visit www.exelixis.com , follow @ExelixisInc on X (Twitter), like Exelixis, Inc. on Facebook and follow Exelixis on LinkedIn. title: Cabaletta Bio Announces Pricing of $150 Million Underwritten Offering
summary: Cabaletta Bio Announces Pricing of $150 Million Underwritten Offering
body_text: Download as PDF May 04, 2026 6:35am EDT PHILADELPHIA, May 04, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Cabaletta Bio, Inc. (“Cabaletta” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: CABA), a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing and launching curative targeted cell therapies designed specifically for patients with autoimmune diseases, announced today the pricing of an underwritten offering of 51,725,000 shares of common stock. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and offering expenses, are expected to be approximately $150 million. The offering is expected to close on or about May 5, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. The financing included participation from Bain Capital Life Sciences, Adage Capital Management, Cormorant Asset Management and other existing investors, multiple new mutual and sovereign wealth funds and Eli Lilly and Company. The purchase price for the common stock is $2.90 per share, which represents the at-the-market price under Nasdaq rules. All of the shares in the offering are being sold by Cabaletta. TD Cowen, Guggenheim Securities, and Cantor are acting as joint book-running managers for the offering. H.C. Wainwright & Co. is acting as lead manager for the offering. The shares of common stock are being offered by Cabaletta pursuant to a shelf registration statement on Form S-3-ASR (File No. 333-278126), as amended by that certain Post-Effective Amendment No. 1 to Form S-3 (No. 333-278126) and that certain Post-Effective Amendment No. 2 to Form S-3 (No. 333-278126), which was declared effective by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on March 31, 2025. The prospectus supplement and accompanying prospectus relating to the offering will be filed with the SEC and will be available on the SEC’s website at www.sec.gov. Copies of the prospectus supplement and accompanying prospectus may also be obtained, when available, by contacting: TD Securities (USA) LLC, c/o Broadridge Financial Solutions, 1155 Long Island Avenue, Edgewood, NY 11717, or by email at TDManualrequest@broadridge.com; Guggenheim Securities, LLC, by mail at Attention: Equity Syndicate Department, 330 Madison Avenue, 8th Floor, New York, NY 10017, by telephone at (212) 518-9544 or by email at GSEquityProspectusDelivery@guggenheimpartners.com; or Cantor Fitzgerald & Co. by mail at Attention: Capital Markets, 110 East 59th Street, 6th Floor, New York 10022 or by email at prospectus@cantor.com. This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction. About Cabaletta Bio Cabaletta Bio (Nasdaq: CABA) is a late clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing and launching curative targeted cell therapies designed specifically for patients with autoimmune diseases. The CABA™ platform encompasses two complementary strategies which aim to advance the discovery and development of engineered T cell therapies with the potential to become deep and durable, perhaps curative, treatments for a broad range of autoimmune diseases. The lead CARTA (Chimeric Antigen Receptor T cells for Autoimmunity) strategy is prioritizing the development of rese-cel, a 4-1BB-containing fully human CD19-CAR T cell investigational therapy. Rese-cel is currently being evaluated in the RESET™ (REstoring SElf-Tolerance) clinical development program spanning multiple therapeutic areas, including rheumatology, neurology and dermatology. Cabaletta Bio’s headquarters and labs are located in Philadelphia, PA. title: Hafnia Wins Marine Money “Deal of the Year” Award
summary: Hafnia has been awarded one of the two prestigious Marine Money “Bank Debt Deal of the Year” Awards for 2025 in recognition of its landmark $715 million Senior Secured Revolver and $417 million Accordion Facility. In announcing the award in May 2026, Marine Money noted that it had evaluated “an extraordinary number of outstanding transactions” for its 2025 […]
body_text: Hafnia has been awarded one of the two prestigious Marine Money “Bank Debt Deal of the Year” Awards for 2025 in recognition of its landmark $715 million Senior Secured Revolver and $417 million Accordion Facility . In announcing the award in May 2026, Marine Money noted that it had evaluated “an extraordinary number of outstanding transactions” for its 2025 Deal of the Year Awards issue. The award highlights Hafnia’s innovative and strategic approach to financing, recognizing the transaction as a standout achievement in the global shipping and banking markets. The winning financing structure was led in partnership with a group of premier international banks, including ING Bank, BNP Paribas, Société Générale, DBS Bank, OCBC, UOB, SEB, Standard Chartered, Taishin International, and E.Sun Commercial. According to Marine Money , the deal was “a case study in the art and strategy of forming bank debt,” praised for optimizing leverage, reducing costs, extending tenor, and creating long-term balance sheet flexibility. Congratulations to everyone involved in delivering this award-winning transaction. More information on the transaction can be read here.
